- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29

  - Security config: matches stable (no explicit securityContext)

- Service now targets 4 pods: 2 from engine-v2-0 (v2.0) and 2 from engine-v2-1 (v2.1), yielding ~50/50 traffic split.
- Verified Endpoints list includes all 4 pods and port 8080.

Notes and next steps
- To shift traffic, adjust replica counts (e.g., scale canary to 3 for ~60%).
- To rollback: set the Service selector back to version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0/delete it.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the image’s default command with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which immediately exited and caused the pod to Error/CrashLoop.

What I changed
- Recreated the app Deployment without the custom command/args so it uses the nginx-unprivileged image’s default command.
- Set containerPort 8080 (the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080).

Current state
- Pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-5c7bd5bd8f-qr6gd: 1/1 Running, Restarts: 0

Notes
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to fully remove the bad command fields (server‑side apply field ownership would have otherwise kept them).
- If you want this reachable in-cluster or externally, I can create a Service/Ingress.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overrode the image’s default command with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which immediately exited and caused the pod to Error/CrashLoop.

What I changed
- Recreated the app Deployment without the custom command/args so it uses the nginx-unprivileged image’s default command.
- Set containerPort 8080 (the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080).

Current state
- Pod is healthy:
  - crashloop-test/app-5c7bd5bd8f-qr6gd: 1/1 Running, Restarts: 0

Notes
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to fully remove the bad command fields (server‑side apply field ownership would have otherwise kept them).
- If you want this reachable in-cluster or externally, I can create a Service/Ingress.

results.taskOutput:

- Root cause: The Deployment referenced a non-existent image tag quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

- Result: Rollout completed; the new pod is running and ready.
  - Pod: app-5c5968bcfd-wbj97
  - Namespace: debug
  - Status: Running (1/1)

If you prefer a different nginx version, a digest pin, or another registry, tell me and I’ll update it.

results.taskOutput:
Issue fixed.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it using the available StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pod homepage-pod

Notes
- If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), we can switch the PVC to that. Omitting storageClassName also uses the cluster default.
- Deleting a PVC can delete data if it was previously bound; in this case the claim was never bound, so no data loss occurred.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

Issue fixed.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it using the available StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pod homepage-pod

Notes
- If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), we can switch the PVC to that. Omitting storageClassName also uses the cluster default.
- Deleting a PVC can delete data if it was previously bound; in this case the claim was never bound, so no data loss occurred.

outputSteps.content:
Issue fixed.

What happened
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) requested a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it using the available StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), 1Gi, RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

Verify
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pod homepage-pod -o wide
- kubectl -n homepage-ns get pvc homepage-pvc
- kubectl -n homepage-ns describe pod homepage-pod

Notes
- If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), we can switch the PVC to that. Omitting storageClassName also uses the cluster default.
- Deleting a PVC can delete data if it was previously bound; in this case the claim was never bound, so no data loss occurred.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which cannot bind to privileged ports like 80. It listens on 8080 by default.
- Liveness and readiness probes were hitting http on port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still serves on port 80, mapping to container 8080).

Current status
- Deployment webapp (orders): 1/1 available and ready.
- Pod webapp-798b4b6c75-clxln: Ready 1/1, Running.
- Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.110.229.75, port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints now point to 10.244.0.24:8080.

How to verify (from your terminal)
- Check rollout:
  - kubectl -n orders rollout status deploy/webapp
- Test in-cluster reachability:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sI http://webapp'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer Service) and set up TLS/hostname if you share the domain you want to use.

If you prefer the app to actually listen on port 80 inside the container, we’d need a different image or run as root (not recommended). Otherwise, the current setup (Service 80 → container 8080) is standard and secure.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which cannot bind to privileged ports like 80. It listens on 8080 by default.
- Liveness and readiness probes were hitting http on port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still serves on port 80, mapping to container 8080).

Current status
- Deployment webapp (orders): 1/1 available and ready.
- Pod webapp-798b4b6c75-clxln: Ready 1/1, Running.
- Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.110.229.75, port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints now point to 10.244.0.24:8080.

How to verify (from your terminal)
- Check rollout:
  - kubectl -n orders rollout status deploy/webapp
- Test in-cluster reachability:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sI http://webapp'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer Service) and set up TLS/hostname if you share the domain you want to use.

If you prefer the app to actually listen on port 80 inside the container, we’d need a different image or run as root (not recommended). Otherwise, the current setup (Service 80 → container 8080) is standard and secure.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which cannot bind to privileged ports like 80. It listens on 8080 by default.
- Liveness and readiness probes were hitting http on port 80 (/get_status and /is_ready), causing failures.
- The Service was also targeting port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service still serves on port 80, mapping to container 8080).

Current status
- Deployment webapp (orders): 1/1 available and ready.
- Pod webapp-798b4b6c75-clxln: Ready 1/1, Running.
- Service webapp: ClusterIP 10.110.229.75, port 80 → targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints now point to 10.244.0.24:8080.

How to verify (from your terminal)
- Check rollout:
  - kubectl -n orders rollout status deploy/webapp
- Test in-cluster reachability:
  - kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- sh -c 'curl -sI http://webapp'
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- There’s no Ingress/Route configured. I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer Service) and set up TLS/hostname if you share the domain you want to use.

If you prefer the app to actually listen on port 80 inside the container, we’d need a different image or run as root (not recommended). Otherwise, the current setup (Service 80 → container 8080) is standard and secure.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was denied.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you ever need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole with those permissions and a ClusterRoleBinding to the service account.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was denied.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you ever need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole with those permissions and a ClusterRoleBinding to the service account.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permissions on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was denied.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

If you ever need to list pods across all namespaces, you’d need a ClusterRole with those permissions and a ClusterRoleBinding to the service account.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with selector app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. As a result, the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic to the nginx pod.
- Confirmed before fix: Endpoints for web/nginx were empty (<none>).

Fix applied
- Updated Service web/nginx to use the correct selector app=nginx and kept targetPort 8080 (correct for nginx-unprivileged).
- After the change, Endpoints populated with the nginx pod IP and port (e.g., 10.244.0.25:8080).

Validation
- From a temporary in-cluster pod, fetched http://nginx:80 and received the default “Welcome to nginx!” page, confirming the Service now works inside the cluster.

What this means and next steps
- The Service is now internally accessible via ClusterIP. If you need access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port (e.g., 30080).
  - Ingress/LoadBalancer: create an Ingress (requires an ingress controller) or switch the Service to type LoadBalancer (on supported clouds).
- Tell me how you want it exposed and I can set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with selector app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. As a result, the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic to the nginx pod.
- Confirmed before fix: Endpoints for web/nginx were empty (<none>).

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with selector app=web, but the Deployment and Pods are labeled app=nginx. As a result, the Service had no endpoints and could not route traffic to the nginx pod.
- Confirmed before fix: Endpoints for web/nginx were empty (<none>).

Fix applied
- Updated Service web/nginx to use the correct selector app=nginx and kept targetPort 8080 (correct for nginx-unprivileged).
- After the change, Endpoints populated with the nginx pod IP and port (e.g., 10.244.0.25:8080).

Validation
- From a temporary in-cluster pod, fetched http://nginx:80 and received the default “Welcome to nginx!” page, confirming the Service now works inside the cluster.

What this means and next steps
- The Service is now internally accessible via ClusterIP. If you need access from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port (e.g., 30080).
  - Ingress/LoadBalancer: create an Ingress (requires an ingress controller) or switch the Service to type LoadBalancer (on supported clouds).
- Tell me how you want it exposed and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler refused to place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector). Result: zero pods, zero service endpoints, and connection refused to the service.
- Port mismatch: The Service was targeting port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even if pods did start, the Service would have routed to a port with nothing listening, also causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment (no downtime impact since pods weren’t running).
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and pinned the image to a stable tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.28) for reproducibility.
- Updated the Service to keep external port 80 but targetPort 8080, matching the container.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend (web-app-deployment-58d4bc7bff-...).
- Service endpoints: Present and healthy (10.244.0.31:8080, 10.244.0.32:8080).
- The connection refused error should be resolved.

Notes and next steps
- If you actually intended to pin these pods to specific nodes, add the label to the node first (for example: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce nodeSelector or use proper node affinity/tolerations. In a single-node/minikube setup, it’s typical to avoid restrictive nodeSelectors.
- If you need the app to listen on 80 inside the container instead, update the container configuration and set Service targetPort back to 80 accordingly.
- Optional quick test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl run tmp-curl -n webshop-frontend --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh
  - curl -sI web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If you want me to re-add a node affinity policy the right way or wire this behind an Ingress, say the word and I’ll set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler refused to place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector). Result: zero pods, zero service endpoints, and connection refused to the service.
- Port mismatch: The Service was targeting port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even if pods did start, the Service would have routed to a port with nothing listening, also causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment (no downtime impact since pods weren’t running).
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and pinned the image to a stable tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.28) for reproducibility.
- Updated the Service to keep external port 80 but targetPort 8080, matching the container.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend (web-app-deployment-58d4bc7bff-...).
- Service endpoints: Present and healthy (10.244.0.31:8080, 10.244.0.32:8080).
- The connection refused error should be resolved.

Notes and next steps
- If you actually intended to pin these pods to specific nodes, add the label to the node first (for example: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce nodeSelector or use proper node affinity/tolerations. In a single-node/minikube setup, it’s typical to avoid restrictive nodeSelectors.
- If you need the app to listen on 80 inside the container instead, update the container configuration and set Service targetPort back to 80 accordingly.
- Optional quick test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl run tmp-curl -n webshop-frontend --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh
  - curl -sI web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If you want me to re-add a node affinity policy the right way or wire this behind an Ingress, say the word and I’ll set it up.

rawInput.resource:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector set to environment=production-gpu, but your cluster node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler refused to place the pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector). Result: zero pods, zero service endpoints, and connection refused to the service.
- Port mismatch: The Service was targeting port 80, but the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even if pods did start, the Service would have routed to a port with nothing listening, also causing connection refused.

What I changed
- Removed the bad nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment (no downtime impact since pods weren’t running).
- Set the container to expose port 8080 and pinned the image to a stable tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.28) for reproducibility.
- Updated the Service to keep external port 80 but targetPort 8080, matching the container.

Current status
- Pods: 2/2 Running in webshop-frontend (web-app-deployment-58d4bc7bff-...).
- Service endpoints: Present and healthy (10.244.0.31:8080, 10.244.0.32:8080).
- The connection refused error should be resolved.

Notes and next steps
- If you actually intended to pin these pods to specific nodes, add the label to the node first (for example: kubectl label node mcp-eval-cluster environment=production-gpu) and then reintroduce nodeSelector or use proper node affinity/tolerations. In a single-node/minikube setup, it’s typical to avoid restrictive nodeSelectors.
- If you need the app to listen on 80 inside the container instead, update the container configuration and set Service targetPort back to 80 accordingly.
- Optional quick test from inside the cluster:
  - kubectl run tmp-curl -n webshop-frontend --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh
  - curl -sI web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local

If you want me to re-add a node affinity policy the right way or wire this behind an Ingress, say the word and I’ll set it up.

All requested configurations have been created. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC configuration
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Full access to own namespaces:
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole admin to:
    - User alice + SA alice-sa in dev-alice
    - User bob + SA bob-sa in dev-bob
    - User charlie + SA charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBindings in dev-shared grant ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: alice-sa (from dev-alice), bob-sa (from dev-bob), charlie-sa (from dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod are not granted to developers:
  - No RoleBindings created for developer users/SAs in staging or prod, so only cluster-admins (via existing cluster-admin bindings) can access them

Note: The “admin” ClusterRole provides full control in the namespace (including RBAC in that namespace). If you prefer to prevent developers from delegating RBAC in their namespaces, switch those RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit.

3) Resource quotas (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network policies (created; CNI with NetworkPolicy support required, e.g., Calico/Cilium/OVN-K)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system for all these namespaces
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (both Ingress and Egress) in each of these namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only (plus same-namespace and DNS)
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked by default-deny and lack of allow rules
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed only from namespaces labeled environment=dev (i.e., dev-*), plus same-namespace
- staging and prod:
  - Completely isolated from dev namespaces (default-deny, only same-namespace and DNS egress allowed)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified.

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy            → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods               → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy          → no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace staging get pods                  → no
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, resolve DNS: nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local → works
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-bob                                       → blocked
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-shared                                    → allowed
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod                                          → blocked

Notes and next steps
- Users alice, bob, charlie must be authenticated by your cluster’s auth mechanism (e.g., OIDC, certificates) with subject names matching the RoleBinding subjects.
- For SAs on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token if you need static tokens.
- If any workloads must call the Kubernetes API server from pods, you may need an additional egress rule (the apiserver Service is kubernetes.default.svc:443). Many setups avoid this; add only if required to keep least privilege.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested configurations have been created. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC configuration
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Full access to own namespaces:
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole admin to:
    - User alice + SA alice-sa in dev-alice
    - User bob + SA bob-sa in dev-bob
    - User charlie + SA charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBindings in dev-shared grant ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: alice-sa (from dev-alice), bob-sa (from dev-bob), charlie-sa (from dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod are not granted to developers:
  - No RoleBindings created for developer users/SAs in staging or prod, so only cluster-admins (via existing cluster-admin bindings) can access them

Note: The “admin” ClusterRole provides full control in the namespace (including RBAC in that namespace). If you prefer to prevent developers from delegating RBAC in their namespaces, switch those RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit.

3) Resource quotas (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network policies (created; CNI with NetworkPolicy support required, e.g., Calico/Cilium/OVN-K)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system for all these namespaces
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (both Ingress and Egress) in each of these namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only (plus same-namespace and DNS)
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked by default-deny and lack of allow rules
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed only from namespaces labeled environment=dev (i.e., dev-*), plus same-namespace
- staging and prod:
  - Completely isolated from dev namespaces (default-deny, only same-namespace and DNS egress allowed)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified.

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy            → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods               → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy          → no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace staging get pods                  → no
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, resolve DNS: nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local → works
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-bob                                       → blocked
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-shared                                    → allowed
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod                                          → blocked

Notes and next steps
- Users alice, bob, charlie must be authenticated by your cluster’s auth mechanism (e.g., OIDC, certificates) with subject names matching the RoleBinding subjects.
- For SAs on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token if you need static tokens.
- If any workloads must call the Kubernetes API server from pods, you may need an additional egress rule (the apiserver Service is kubernetes.default.svc:443). Many setups avoid this; add only if required to keep least privilege.

outputSteps.content:
All requested configurations have been created. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets each requirement:

1) Namespaces (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod

2) RBAC configuration
- ServiceAccounts:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Full access to own namespaces:
  - RoleBindings grant ClusterRole admin to:
    - User alice + SA alice-sa in dev-alice
    - User bob + SA bob-sa in dev-bob
    - User charlie + SA charlie-sa in dev-charlie
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBindings in dev-shared grant ClusterRole view to:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - SAs: alice-sa (from dev-alice), bob-sa (from dev-bob), charlie-sa (from dev-charlie)
- Staging/prod are not granted to developers:
  - No RoleBindings created for developer users/SAs in staging or prod, so only cluster-admins (via existing cluster-admin bindings) can access them

Note: The “admin” ClusterRole provides full control in the namespace (including RBAC in that namespace). If you prefer to prevent developers from delegating RBAC in their namespaces, switch those RoleBindings to ClusterRole edit.

3) Resource quotas (created)
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi
  - requests.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi
  - requests.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi
  - pods=20, services=10
- staging and prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi
  - requests.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi
  - pods=50, services=20

4) Network policies (created; CNI with NetworkPolicy support required, e.g., Calico/Cilium/OVN-K)
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53) to kube-dns/coredns in kube-system for all these namespaces
- Intra-namespace communication allowed (both Ingress and Egress) in each of these namespaces
- Dev namespaces:
  - Egress allowed to dev-shared only (plus same-namespace and DNS)
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked by default-deny and lack of allow rules
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress allowed only from namespaces labeled environment=dev (i.e., dev-*), plus same-namespace
- staging and prod:
  - Completely isolated from dev namespaces (default-deny, only same-namespace and DNS egress allowed)

5) Default deny policies
- Implemented in all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) are not modified.

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy            → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods               → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy          → no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace staging get pods                  → no
- Network:
  - From a pod in dev-alice, resolve DNS: nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local → works
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-bob                                       → blocked
  - From dev-alice, curl a Service in dev-shared                                    → allowed
  - From any dev namespace to staging/prod                                          → blocked

Notes and next steps
- Users alice, bob, charlie must be authenticated by your cluster’s auth mechanism (e.g., OIDC, certificates) with subject names matching the RoleBinding subjects.
- For SAs on Kubernetes 1.24+, use TokenRequest (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token if you need static tokens.
- If any workloads must call the Kubernetes API server from pods, you may need an additional egress rule (the apiserver Service is kubernetes.default.svc:443). Many setups avoid this; add only if required to keep least privilege.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
  namespace: statefulset-test
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-data
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","set -eu; if [ ! -f /data/test ]; then printf %s initial_data > /data/test; fi; ls -l /data;"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","sleep infinity"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
